name: Greek Meander
basis: running key-pattern unit with paint width from tone (how)
note: Offers black-figure and red-figure colour schemes but models no slip painting.

lumenary.blurb: The key pattern painted around Athenian pots. Rows of unbroken fret run across the clay, and the line is drawn thicker where your picture is darker and thinner where it is light.

facts.era: From about the ninth century BCE

why: The meander, or Greek key, is a line that runs round and round without ever breaking, turning back on itself at right angles. The name comes from the river Maiandros, which winds. It frames Greek pots as a band of unbroken fret, and here the paint is thicker where your picture is darker, so the picture appears in the weight of the line.
how: Draw a key unit in a band six units high: the line goes up the left side, along the top, down the right, back toward the left, up again and then a short way right, and sits on a rule at the bottom.
Repeat the unit every eight units, with alternate bands mirrored and shifted by half a period.
Read the shade v at the middle of each segment and set the paint width from it.
Offer three styles: black-figure (black slip on red-orange clay), red-figure (a black ground with the clay left showing) and white ground.
Add rule lines and tint the clay from the picture.
history: The key pattern runs round Greek pots from the geometric period onward, and later it was used by the Romans and revived in neoclassical architecture and fashion. Black-figure vases were painted in Corinth and Athens from the seventh century BCE, and the red-figure technique appeared in Athens around 520 BCE. The river Maiandros is now the Büyük Menderes in Turkey, and gave its name to the English word meander.
uses: Borders for pottery, textiles and architecture
Logos and branding with a classical air
terms: A winding line, from the river Maiandros, or the fret pattern named after it.
Vase painting in which figures are painted in black on a clay ground.
A watery clay used for painting pottery before firing.
paragraphs: The meander takes its name from the river Maiandros, which winds. The key pattern runs round Greek pots from the geometric period onward. In black-figure vases the painter draws in a slip that fires black on the red-orange clay. In red-figure vases the ground is painted black and the figures are left in the colour of the clay, and the program offers both, together with a white-ground style. A key unit is drawn in a band six units high. Its line goes up the left side, along the top, down the right, back toward the left, up again and then a short way right, and sits on a rule at the bottom. The unit repeats every eight units, and alternate bands are mirrored and shifted by half a period.

The width of the paint follows the picture. Each segment of the pattern reads the shade v at its middle, which is the darkness of the picture for black paint and the brightness for red-figure, and draws its line with a width between 0.18 and about 1.2 units. Dark places get thick, heavy fret and light places a thread. The hook is made of straight segments of lengths 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1.5, which is 21.5 units, and with the rule underneath and the pair of border rules the paint covers a fraction of the band that grows with the line width. The clay itself is mottled, and a share of the picture is multiplied into it (screened on the black ground of the red-figure style).

equations.note: Line width at a segment: β is the weight slider and f the weight-follows-picture slider.
Length of line in one 8 u by 9 u cell: the hook, the rule it stands on, and the two border rules.
The share of the clay covered by paint: about 11% at the thinnest line and up to 75% at the heaviest, which is how the line weight draws the picture.

presets.text: Red-figure reverses the black and the clay.
White ground looks like a funeral vase.
Small keys form a dense frieze.
